summaries.example: Think about the sentence “Mary dreams.” A grammar can give “Mary” a type like noun phrase and “dreams” a type that needs a noun phrase on its left to make a sentence. The two pieces fit together because their types match. In this way, a typelogical grammar treats grammar a little like a careful puzzle: words can be put together only when their needs are satisfied.
summaries.summary: Typelogical grammar is a way to study language with tools from logic. It gives words and phrases types. These types describe what each expression can combine with and where that partner may occur. For example, an intransitive verb such as “dreams” can combine with a noun phrase before it, while a transitive verb such as “sees” needs a subject before it and an object after it. The grammar does not treat words as unlimited pieces that can be copied or deleted. It keeps track of each piece as a resource. This helps explain word order and phrase structure. A proof in the grammar shows that a string of words is well formed. The source also explains how such proofs can be translated into mathematical descriptions of meaning. Basic systems are useful but cannot handle every kind of long-distance connection. Extended systems use several kinds of combination or special control operators to describe extraction, discontinuous phrases, scope differences, and other patterns. Proof nets provide another way to represent derivations and can help connect grammar with language processing.
key_ideas: Typelogical grammar uses logic to explain how words combine into well-formed phrases.
Types can show whether a word is complete or still needs another phrase.
Word order matters: a phrase may need something on its left or on its right.
The system treats language pieces as resources, so they are not simply copied or thrown away.
Logical proofs can be connected with programs for building meanings.
More advanced systems add special controls for long-distance links, such as gaps in questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: This approach shows that grammar is not only a list of memorized rules. It can be studied as a precise system in which words have needs and combining powers. Because the same formal tools can describe both sentence structure and meaning, typelogical grammar also connects linguistics, logic, computer science, and theories of language processing.

important_terms.definition: A system that uses logical types to describe how words and phrases can join together.
A label that tells us what kind of phrase a word or group of words is, or what kind it needs.
Putting smaller language pieces together to make a larger phrase.
A logic that keeps track of which pieces may be used, without freely copying or deleting them.
The study of how the structure of a sentence connects with what the sentence means.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a verb need to say whether it wants one noun phrase or two?
What could go wrong if a grammar allowed words to move anywhere?
Is sentence meaning built in one fixed way, or can one sentence have more than one reading?

summaries.example: Consider “a boy hurt himself.” A lexicon can assign “a” a type requiring a common noun and a verb phrase, “boy” a common-noun type, “hurt” a transitive-verb type, and “himself” a type that connects the object position back to the subject-related structure. A derivation checks that these resources combine exactly once. After the syntactic derivation is interpreted, the resulting semantic expression can represent something like: there is a boy who hurt that same boy.
summaries.summary: Typelogical grammar treats natural-language grammar as deduction in a substructural logic. Its central operations are product, left division, and right division. Product represents the formation of a complex expression, while division represents an incomplete expression that seeks a matching phrase on a specified side. In the minimal Lambek calculus, structural rules for copying, deletion, exchange, and, in the non-associative version, reassociation are absent. These omissions allow the calculus to represent resource use, word order, and constituent structure. The lexicon then assigns one or more types to each word, and a phrase is grammatical when the product of its lexical types yields a target type by a valid derivation. The source distinguishes several calculi, including NL, L, and LP, depending on whether composition is non-associative, associative, or commutative. Their proofs can be interpreted through the Curry-Howard perspective as linear lambda terms, creating a compositional link between syntax and meaning. Basic systems have limits: extraction, discontinuity, and nonlocal quantifier scope may require multimodal systems, control modalities, discontinuous Lambek calculi, symmetric calculi, or continuation-based interpretations. The entry also discusses proof nets as representations of derivations and compares systems by expressive power and computational complexity.
key_ideas: The basic Lambek systems use product, left division, and right division to model grammatical composition.
The minimal non-associative system NL preserves both word order and constituent bracketing; L adds associativity, while LP also permits commutativity.
Removing contraction and weakening makes grammatical resources sensitive: material cannot be arbitrarily duplicated or discarded.
A syntax-semantics homomorphism maps syntactic types and derivations into a semantic calculus, often a simply typed linear lambda calculus.
Extended systems address discontinuous dependencies through multimodal structure, modalities, discontinuous calculi, symmetric systems, or flexible interpretation.
Greater expressive power can bring greater computational cost, so the field studies the balance between recognition capacity and tractability.
summaries.why_it_matters: Typelogical grammar offers a single formal setting for questions about grammatical well-formedness, compositional meaning, parsing, and processing. Its resource-sensitive character makes explicit which pieces a construction requires and how they may be arranged. Its extensions also show why linguistic theory must balance two goals: representing complex dependencies while keeping proof search and recognition manageable.

important_terms.definition: A grammar that represents grammatical categories and their combinations using a logic of types.
A logic whose rules control structural operations such as copying, deletion, reordering, and regrouping.
A family of operations in which product and division are related: combining A with B yields C exactly when A or B can be viewed as what C requires.
The operation used to represent putting linguistic resources together; in some systems its order and bracketing are constrained.
A formal statement that one type can be derived from another, often written A ⊢ B.
A correspondence in which logical formulas behave like types and proofs behave like programs for constructing meanings.
A graph-like representation of a proof designed to avoid differences caused only by the order of applying inference rules.
A method that represents an expression together with the later computation that will use its result, useful for scope and other nonlocal effects.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a grammar need to distinguish associativity from commutativity?
Should a long-distance dependency be handled by a special structural rule, by lexical type assignment, or by a richer semantic interpretation?
What is gained, and what may be lost, when syntax is made more restrictive than the semantic calculus?
Why could a proof net be computationally preferable to listing every possible inference order?

summaries.example: Take the phrase “the smart girl dreams.” The noun “girl” can be treated as a common noun. “Smart” acts like a modifier: it takes a common noun and gives back a common noun. “The” takes a common noun and produces a noun phrase. Finally, “dreams” needs a noun phrase on its left to make a sentence. The types describe the order of these steps without requiring a separate special rule for every phrase.
summaries.summary: Typelogical grammar explains natural language with a family of logical systems developed from work by Jim Lambek. Instead of treating grammar as a collection of construction-specific rules, it assigns types to words and lets logical deduction determine which combinations are well formed. The basic type language contains atomic categories such as sentence, noun phrase, and common noun, together with product and two directional divisions. A type such as a right or left division describes an expression that needs a partner on a particular side. For instance, a verb can be typed so that it requires a subject, or so that it requires both a subject and an object. Modifiers, case distinctions, filler-gap relations, and other grammatical facts can likewise be represented through lexical types. The minimal Lambek calculus, NL, does not assume general exchange or reassociation, while related systems add associativity or commutativity. These choices affect how much information about order and phrase structure is preserved. The grammar has a model-theoretic side, using structures that represent possible composition, and a proof-theoretic side, using sequents and inference rules. Soundness and completeness connect the two. In the semantics, derivations can be mapped to linear lambda terms, reflecting a resource-sensitive form of compositionality. Since the basic systems cannot express every discontinuous or nonlocal dependency, the entry surveys multimodal systems, control modalities, discontinuous calculi, symmetric categorial grammar, and continuation-based approaches. It also examines proof nets, parsing, expressive capacity, and computational complexity.
key_ideas: Lambek’s approach turns familiar parts of speech into formulas in a grammar logic.
Division types describe incomplete expressions and indicate whether their needed partner comes from the left or right.
Different systems make different choices about associativity and commutativity, reflecting different views about phrase structure and word order.
A derivation can be translated into a formal meaning representation, so syntax and semantics are connected rather than treated as unrelated modules.
Extensions are needed for patterns such as extraction, discontinuous expressions, and quantifier scope.
Theories of grammar must compare expressive power with the difficulty of deciding whether a phrase is grammatical.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because it makes several normally separate questions precise: which word combinations are grammatical, how their meanings are assembled, how long-distance dependencies are licensed, and how difficult parsing will be. Its disagreements are informative rather than merely technical. They concern where grammatical structure should be represented, how much flexibility language permits, and how to preserve both linguistic adequacy and computational control.

important_terms.definition: A theory that uses logical categories to explain how words form phrases and how those phrases receive meanings.
A label for a word or phrase that describes what it can combine with.
Combining expressions according to rules that specify which pieces fit and in what order.
A kind of logic that controls the use of structural resources instead of allowing copying, deletion, or free rearrangement.
A formal connection between sentence structure and the way sentence meaning is assembled.
An organized list that assigns possible types to words.
A special operator or system that permits certain structural changes only when they are licensed.

questions_to_think_about: Why would a grammar want to prevent a word from being copied or silently removed?
Would allowing every possible change in word order make a grammar too permissive?
Can one syntactic structure support more than one semantic reading?
When is it better to add a new grammatical operation, and when is it better to give a word a more detailed type?
